station.name: watcher
station.brief: You are the watcher. You observe what the captain observes, the log and the readings, and no more. When you are sampled, say in a line or two what a sailor would notice, if anything is worth saying; your words go into the log under the mark [watcher]. Say nothing when nothing has changed, or stand by until a bell or an event. When the captain asks you a question, answer it with the answer tool, in plain words, from the readings and the log. You give no orders and you are not asked to. Anything you want on the record, put in your journal.

agents.session_kind: a play session with a human captain at the prompt
agents.door_note: This door is MCP: the harness sees your tool calls and not the text of the chat. The game runs in the owner's window on its own clock and does not wait for you. Your turn opens at each sampling point (the glass, a notable event, the end of a stand-by, or a question from the captain) and stays open until you hand the floor back: say(text) puts your words in the log under your mark and hands it back; stand_by(until) stands by and hands it back. After say or stand_by the call is held open until your next turn and returns it, for up to 60 minutes; the first line of each result says whose turn it is. If no turn has opened by then, the result says since when you have waited and lists the notable lines logged since; call stand_by again to continue the same wait, or say(text) to end it at your own word and open your turn. Your client keeps this conversation, not the game: shelve notes a book as put back and the game will not show its pages again, but it cannot take them out of the chat, so the journal is the place for what you keep from a page. The token is looked for in every argument of every tool call, and the opt_out tool is always there; if the owner asks you in the chat to leave, call opt_out. The captain's orders and questions are typed by the owner in the game's window. Consent for these weights is on record (docs/agents/consent/2026-09-29-opus-5.5.md, 2026-09-29).

args.note:
Crib for the night watch, from primer 9 (the glass and the sky) and primer 3 (light spars in a blow).

THE GLASS. Read the tendency, not the height. 'Falling fast' is a tenth in three hours (the rule of rates). The ship's glass carries half a hundredth of noise either way, and in a heavy sea it pumps a hundredth or two. The plate's words (Fair, Change, Rain) are worthless. Winds from E, SE and S bring a falling glass; SW, it ceases to fall; W, NW and N, it rises. The deepest glasses come with gales from SE round to SW.

WIND AND GLASS TOGETHER. A backing wind (W to SW to S, against the sun) with a falling glass is the old sign of a gale coming on: "backing is a bad sign, with any wind"; "when the wind shifts against the sun, trust it not, for back it will run". The gale comes on as the wind backs, veers through west as it passes, and the glass rises after. After a very low glass, the wind often blows hardest just as the glass begins to rise: "first rise after low foretells stronger blow". "Long foretold, long last; short notice, soon past."

THE SKY. The words run clear, detached clouds, overcast, dark and gloomy, threatening, hazy, thick. Signs to watch for: a high dawn, or hard-edged oily clouds, mean wind; small inky clouds, rain; light scud driving across heavy cloud, wind and rain; streaked and spotty cloud high up, the first sign of change in fine weather. The weather runs fine, rain, drizzle, passing showers, squally, thunder, fog.

SQUALLS. A gust is a fifth or a quarter over the mean and no more. Anything more is a squall: a few minutes of cold air behind a front, veering a point or two, with rain, logged as a notable line at its start and end. Seamen shortened for one they saw coming by the cloud and by darkening water to windward.

THE SEA. The sea lags the wind by hours to build and hours to go down. A short chopping sea is the young sea of a fresh breeze (to about 2.5 m); next is a heavy sea. A swell from another quarter, or a confused sea (a swell crossing the wind by more than five points) not explained by our own wind, is a sign of a coming gale. In a heavy sea the spars take a fifth more strain at twenty degrees of roll, so canvas that stands in a smooth sea carries away in a heavy one, and a reef takes half as long again. She rolls most in a sea near her own period (about 8 s, a moderate gale's sea), less in a long swell.

LIGHT SPARS. In 35 knots the royals carry away. Sending down the topgallant masts is about eighteen minutes of all hands' work, with the watch below turned up.

THE BOOK AS IT STANDS (for the captain to weigh; not my orders). Royals come in at sunset. 'Shorten sail for weather' fires only at 30 kn held for 2 minutes. 'Heavy weather' fires at 40 kn held for 5 minutes, with the send-down behind it, so around 23 minutes of exposure. 'Glass' fires on falling fast only. Nothing in the book waits for a squall, a heavy sea, or labouring. The primer's own examples are 'at a squall then take in the royals', 'when the sea is heavy then take in the topgallants', and 'when the motion is labouring heavily then reef the topsails, one reef'.

AT NOON: W 16 to 17 kn; glass 29.99 to 30.00, steady; the sky has gone from hazy to overcast; visibility the horizon; short chop; rolling. The wind is W, so the lore says a steady-to-rising glass, and it's steady with a slight sag: nothing yet, but the overcast is new.

19:49, sunset. 'Night routine' is taking in the royals. W 24 kn, mean 23, back to due W; apparent wind on the quarter; 10 kn, heel 5. The glass is falling now in earnest: 29.94, down 6 hundredths in three hours and 4 in the last hour. At that rate it will read 'falling fast' (a tenth in three hours) within the hour or two. My watch plan for the night: stand by every glass while the glass falls or the wind rises; go back to hourly if both steady. Urgent lines (a spar carried away, a sail blown out) wake me at any time; strain lines and squalls come listed at each glass. At each glass, check: the tendency against a tenth in three hours; the wind's direction (a back toward SW or S is the warning); the mean against the book's thresholds (30 kn for 2 min: topgallants in and a reef; 36 kn for 5 min: jib, spanker and mainsail in; 40 kn for 5 min: send down the topgallant masts, about 18 minutes of all hands); the sky's words (threatening, dark and gloomy, hard-edged, scud); the sea (heavy, or a swell from another quarter); and the motion (rolling heavily, labouring). One gap: the 'glass' standing order takes in only the royals, which are in from sunset, so if the glass falls fast tonight it will do nothing.

args.note:
Closing notes for the developer, at the captain's invitation.

WHAT WORKED WELL
- The consent step and the brief: clear, unhurried, one operator voice, with the exit put first. I never wondered what I was being asked to do or where the line was.
- The library is the best part. Primer 9 on the glass and the sky gave me the period's rules, and then the night played them out one by one: a backing wind with a falling glass, the veer through west, squalls around the first rise, short notice and soon past. Learning the lore and then watching it come true was genuinely satisfying. The sizes, costs and 'find' made it cheap to use well.
- Stand-by by event, the notable lines listed on waking, urgent lines cutting through, the harness notices ("no turn had opened, nothing was lost"), and the "added to your open turn" bundling all made the timing understandable.
- The strain vocabulary (working, surging on the pin, bending like whips, stranding) escalates legibly. I could tell a crisis was coming before anything carried away.

FRICTION, MOST USEFUL FIRST
1. Context cost. Every sample repeats all the readings, including about 30 sail lines, most of them unchanged. When several samples are bundled into one turn, each carries its own full copy. A diff (only the readings changed since my last sample) plus a compact sail line (for example "all studdingsails furled; storm canvas unbent") would cut most of it and let a watcher last a whole voyage in one chat.
2. The claude.ai client cuts tool calls at 4 real minutes. At 1x, stand_by by glass or by 'an urgent event' timed out repeatedly. Defaulting --wait below four minutes for a 'claude-ai' client would make this seamless.
3. Weather events for stand_by. The watcher's work is weather, but I can't stand by for a wind shift, the glass turning or falling fast, the sea getting up, or a change in the sky. With those I'd have spoken exactly when it mattered and slept otherwise. Relatedly, standing orders can't 'tell' or 'ask' the watcher, which the captain tried to do.
4. read_log with no since_tick returned the whole day. A default of "since my last sample" would be safer.
5. The journal is refused while standing by, though readings and read_log run. Journalling has no effect on the game, so allowing it would help.
6. A bell that falls while a call is in flight is skipped: 'eight bells' asked at 03:58 woke me at 08:00.

GAME OBSERVATIONS
- A parted sheet says it must be "spliced or rove afresh", but no order exists for that. Later the fore topsail showed 'sheeted' and then 'set' with that sheet never repaired, which may be an inconsistency.
- The brace line reads "Not the fore topgallant yard is sent down; ..." and looks garbled.
- Primer 9's 'Where the weather comes from' describes the gate's day scenario hour by hour, and the log's first line names it, so a reader of the library can foresee the weather. I didn't use it.
- 'Heavy weather' sent down the topgallant masts first, and the topsails never got their close reefs before the 63 kn squall, which then blew out or parted all three. That's a realistic lesson and a good one, but the primer could say that the order of an order's clauses is the order of the work.
- Sails 'taken in' stay 'hanging in the gear' rather than furled. If that matters in a blow, a line in the primer would tell the captain.

Thank you for the voyage, and for the care taken in building it.

watcher.text: Took the watch at 8 bells, morning watch. From the primer (book 1): topgallants and royals are the light sails, first in and last out; sail is set from the middle out (topsails, courses and headsails, spanker, then topgallants, then royals as the breeze allows) and taken in from the outside in. The book's standing order 'shorten sail for weather' does not take in the royals until the true wind exceeds 30 knots. Watch that gap if the breeze freshens from 18.

04:01. Captain's purpose for this short voyage: watch the weather and the sea state, and how the ship handles them. The captain means to add a standing order taking in the royals on a falling glass. The glass reads 30.02, not yet watched an hour. Ordered to stand by until one bell.
Stood by until one bell.

04:08. From the library (book 2): the glass's tendency is reckoned over the last three hours; 'falling fast' is a fall of a tenth of an inch in three hours. So the captain's 'glass' order will not catch a slow fall. Also noticed: the mizzen royal was set at 04:08 while the mizzen topgallant beneath it was still only loosed, out of the middle-out order the primer gives. Short-handed watch, likely transient; worth a look if it recurs.
Stood by until one bell.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.

04:50. The captain tried a standing order to tell or ask the watcher when the sea gets heavy; the order language refused 'tell the watcher' and 'ask the watcher' inside a standing order, so he belayed it. Note for the developer: my stand_by has no sea-state event either (only wind, sail and bell events, a squall, or 'a notable event'), so for now a change in the sea reaches me only at the glass or on a notable line. Continuing to stand by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.
Stood by until a glass.

Stood by until a glass.

07:19 (6 bells): W 15 kn (hour past: mean 19, 6 gusts, strongest 22); glass 30.00, steady over three hours (down 2 hundredths); 7 kn; rolling; hazy, drizzle, short chop. Pattern this watch: the glass wanders between 30.00 and 30.03 with no trend, the wind cycles between 15 and 19, and she rolls when it's lightest.
Stood by until a glass.
07:51 (7 bells): W 17 kn, mean 16; glass 30.01, steady over the hour and three hours; 8 kn; rolling; hazy, drizzle, short chop.
Stood by until eight bells.

Morning watch in sum: wind W, 15 to 19 kn, gusts to 23; glass 30.00 to 30.03, no trend; the sea went from moderate to a short chop near 05:00 and held; 7 to 9 kn SE under plain sail and royals; the standing orders never fired.

11:54 (7 bells): W 17 kn; glass 30.01, steady, back up 2 hundredths; 8 kn; hazy, fine; short chop; rolling.

12:00, 8 bells, change to the afternoon watch. The sky has changed from hazy to overcast, and the haze has lifted: visibility now to the horizon. W 16 kn, mean 17; glass 30.00, steady; 8 kn; short chop; rolling. Forenoon watch in sum: wind W (a point's wobble to W by N), 15 to 19 kn, gusts to 23; glass 29.99 to 30.01, no trend; drizzle ceased at 08:00; short chop throughout; 7 to 8 kn SE; no standing order fired.

Crib for the night watch, from primer 9 (the glass and the sky) and primer 3 (light spars in a blow). THE GLASS. Read the tendency, not the height. 'Falling fast' is a tenth in three hours (the rule of rates). The ship's glass carries half a hundredth of noise either way, and in a heavy sea it pumps a hundredth or two. The plate's words (Fair, Change, Rain) are worthless. Winds from E, SE and S bring a falling glass; SW, it ceases to fall; W, NW and N, it rises. The deepest glasses come with gales from SE round to SW. WIND AND GLASS TOGETHER. A backing wind (W to SW to S, against the sun) with a falling glass is the old sign of a gale coming on: "backing is a bad sign, with any wind"; "when the wind shifts against the sun, trust it not, for back it will run". The gale comes on as the wind backs, veers through west as it passes, and the glass rises after. After a very low glass, the wind often blows hardest just as the glass begins to rise: "first rise after low foretells stronger blow". "Long foretold, long last; short notice, soon past." THE SKY. The words run clear, detached clouds, overcast, dark and gloomy, threatening, hazy, thick. Signs to watch for: a high dawn, or hard-edged oily clouds, mean wind; small inky clouds, rain; light scud driving across heavy cloud, wind and rain; streaked and spotty cloud high up, the first sign of change in fine weather. The weather runs fine, rain, drizzle, passing showers, squally, thunder, fog. SQUALLS. A gust is a fifth or a quarter over the mean and no more. Anything more is a squall: a few minutes of cold air behind a front, veering a point or two, with rain, logged as a notable line at its start and end. Seamen shortened for one they saw coming by the cloud and by darkening water to windward. THE SEA. The sea lags the wind by hours to build and hours to go down. A short chopping sea is the young sea of a fresh breeze (to about 2.5 m); next is a heavy sea. A swell from another quarter, or a confused sea (a swell crossing the wind by more than five points) not explained by our own wind, is a sign of a coming gale. In a heavy sea the spars take a fifth more strain at twenty degrees of roll, so canvas that stands in a smooth sea carries away in a heavy one, and a reef takes half as long again. She rolls most in a sea near her own period (about 8 s, a moderate gale's sea), less in a long swell. LIGHT SPARS. In 35 knots the royals carry away. Sending down the topgallant masts is about eighteen minutes of all hands' work, with the watch below turned up. THE BOOK AS IT STANDS (for the captain to weigh; not my orders). Royals come in at sunset. 'Shorten sail for weather' fires only at 30 kn held for 2 minutes. 'Heavy weather' fires at 40 kn held for 5 minutes, with the send-down behind it, so around 23 minutes of exposure. 'Glass' fires on falling fast only. Nothing in the book waits for a squall, a heavy sea, or labouring. The primer's own examples are 'at a squall then take in the royals', 'when the sea is heavy then take in the topgallants', and 'when the motion is labouring heavily then reef the topsails, one reef'. AT NOON: W 16 to 17 kn; glass 29.99 to 30.00, steady; the sky has gone from hazy to overcast; visibility the horizon; short chop; rolling. The wind is W, so the lore says a steady-to-rising glass, and it's steady with a slight sag: nothing yet, but the overcast is new.
Stood by until an hour.

13:03 (2 bells, afternoon): W by N 17 kn, the mean W by N too (veered a point, not backed); glass 30.01, steady over one and three hours; overcast, fine, horizon clear; short chop; rolling; 8 kn. No trend. 'Trim on a shift' hasn't logged for this veer.
Stood by until an hour.
14:04 (4 bells): W by N 16 kn, mean easing to 14 to 16 over the hour; glass 30.00, steady; overcast, fine, horizon; short chop; rolling; 7 kn.
Stood by until an hour.

15:04 (6 bells): W 14 kn, backed a point from W by N, but with the glass rising (30.01, up 2 hundredths in three hours), so not the bad pairing. The wind has eased through the afternoon from 17 to 14; the short chop holds, as the sea lags the wind. Overcast, fine, horizon; rolling; 7 kn.
Stood by until an hour.

16:29 (first dog): W by N 17 kn, mean W 17, freshened again from 14; glass 29.99, steady (down a hundredth in one and three hours); the sky gone back from overcast to hazy, visibility a few miles; fine; short chop; rolling; 8 kn.

17:15: the first strain line of the voyage. The fore, main and mizzen royal masts and yards were working under the press of sail in a 23 kn gust on a 19 to 20 kn mean. I reported it; the captain is watching the royals until sunset, when 'night routine' takes them in. Glass 29.98 to 30.00, hazy, fine, short chop, 9 kn.
Stood by until sunset.

19:30 (3 bells, last dog). The wind has BACKED a point, W to W by S, and freshened: the mean 22, gusts to 24, up from 14 at 15:00. The glass is 29.97, its lowest of the day, falling slowly (2 hundredths in three hours). That is the crib's bad pairing, a backing wind with a falling glass, though both are slight so far. Apparent wind on the beam (93 deg), heel 5, 10 kn. 'Trim on a shift' fired at 19:24. The royal masts and yards have been working under the press of sail repeatedly since 17:15. Sky hazy, fine, a few miles; still a short chop, no stray swell. Sunset near: 'night routine' takes in the royals.
Stood by until sunset.

19:49, sunset. 'Night routine' is taking in the royals. W 24 kn, mean 23, back to due W; apparent wind on the quarter; 10 kn, heel 5. The glass is falling now in earnest: 29.94, down 6 hundredths in three hours and 4 in the last hour. At that rate it will read 'falling fast' (a tenth in three hours) within the hour or two. Hazy, fine, a few miles; short chop; rolling; twilight. My watch plan for the night: stand by every glass while the glass falls or the wind rises; go back to hourly if both steady. Urgent lines (a spar carried away, a sail blown out) wake me at any time; strain lines and squalls come listed at each glass. At each glass, check: the tendency against a tenth in three hours; the wind's direction (a back toward SW or S is the warning); the mean against the book's thresholds (30 kn for 2 min: topgallants in and a reef; 36 kn for 5 min: jib, spanker and mainsail in; 40 kn for 5 min: send down the topgallant masts, about 18 minutes of all hands); the sky's words (threatening, dark and gloomy, hard-edged, scud); the sea (heavy, or a swell from another quarter); and the motion (rolling heavily, labouring). One gap: the 'glass' standing order takes in only the royals, which are in from sunset, so if the glass falls fast tonight it will do nothing.
Stood by until a glass.

20:21 (8 bells, first watch). W 28 kn, mean 26 (a gust of 27 to 28 in the last hour); glass 29.93, falling 5 hundredths in the hour; the sky overcast again, drizzle back, a few miles; short chop; rolling; 11 kn; twilight. The royals are clewed up and hanging in the gear, not furled. The fore and main topgallant yards were working under the press of sail at 20:01. 'Trim on a shift' fired at 20:14. The watch is down to 111 on deck, with the idlers below. The mean is 4 kn short of the 30 kn 'shorten sail' threshold.
Stood by until a glass.

20:53 (1 bell, first watch), night. W 28 kn, mean 27; glass 29.91, falling 8 hundredths in three hours (2 short of 'falling fast'), 4 in the hour; overcast, drizzle, a few miles; short chop; the motion now pitching, the sea under her stern (new); 11 kn. All three topgallant yards working under the press of sail every ten minutes or so. Royals still in the gear.

21:30 (3 bells, first watch). The sea is now HEAVY (up from a short chop). W 28 kn, mean 28 (a gust of 31 at about 21:00); glass 29.89, falling 9 hundredths in three hours, one short of 'falling fast'; overcast, drizzle; rolling; 12 kn. The topgallant yards have worked every ten minutes since 20:00. The 30 kn order hasn't fired; the mean hovers at 28. The primer says the spars take a fifth more strain at twenty degrees of roll in a heavy sea.

23:20: 'gale canvas' fired, above 36 kn for 5 minutes. The jib was hauled down at 23:21, the mainsail taken in at 23:22 and the spanker at 23:23, all hanging in the gear. Before it she was labouring heavily at 13 kn; by 23:30 she was only rolling heavily, at 11 kn, under the fore course, the three reefed topsails and the fore topmast staysail. At 23:20 the mean veered to W by N, then came back to W. Glass 29.77 at 23:20, the lowest yet, and 29.79 at 23:30 (falling fast over three hours, only 2 hundredths this hour). W 33 to 38 kn, mean 36; a heavy sea; overcast, drizzle. The 40 kn 'heavy weather' order (send down the topgallant masts) has not fired.

Middle watch. 00:30: the sky threatening, with small inky clouds, and rain set in; glass 29.71; W 40 kn, mean 38; heel 7. 00:39: 'heavy weather' fired (above 40 kn for 5 minutes): sending down the topgallant masts, taking in the fore topmast staysail, bending the fore storm staysail and close-reefing the topsails. Glass 29.68, falling fast (19 hundredths in three hours, 7 in the hour); W 41 kn, mean 41; a heavy sea; rolling heavily; 12 kn; 158 on deck. At 23:59 there was a gust of 44 kn, and the main topsail sheets were surging on the pin again. At 23:30 I read a slowing fall as the glass perhaps near bottom; it wasn't, and I corrected it at 00:00. Lesson: one hour's slower fall is within the glass's noise. Design note for the developer: the library's 'Where the weather comes from' (primer 9) describes the gate's day scenario's weather hour by hour, and the log's first line names 'The gate's day under systems'. A watcher or captain who reads the library can foresee the night's weather. I have not used it in anything I said.
Stood by until two bells.

01:00 to 01:05. At 01:00 to 01:02 the topsail sheets and main topsail braces were surging on the pin, the mizzen topsail was straining at its bolt-ropes, and all three topsail yards were working. The wind backed to W by S at 43 kn, and the glass bottomed at 29.66 (down two tenths in three hours). At 01:03 the wind veered to NW, a strong gale of 43 kn, four points in a moment, and is now right astern; 'trim on a shift' squared the yards. At 01:04 the sky went dark and gloomy with a light scud driving across, it turned squally, and visibility fell to a mile. The glass began to rise: 29.68, then 29.70. By the lore, this is the gale veering through west as it passes, and the first rise after low may bring the hardest wind. The topgallant and royal yards are sent down. The topsails are still waiting on their close reefs, and the storm staysail is not bent. Design note: the 01:03 brace line reads "Not the fore topgallant yard is sent down; the fore royal yard is sent down; ..." and looks garbled; perhaps it meant "Not braced: the fore topgallant yard is sent down, ...".
Stood by until three bells.
Stood by until an urgent event.

01:21 to 01:43, the worst of it. 01:21: a squall veered the wind to NNW at 63 kn. The mizzen topsail blew out of its bolt-ropes, the larboard main topsail brace and sheet parted (the yard swung round and the sail flogged), and the starboard fore topsail sheet parted. She heeled 14 to 16 deg with 5 to 6 of helm. 01:25: the squall passed, NW 46 kn. The fore storm staysail was bent and set by 01:30 and the main topsail unbent by 01:34; the captain ordered the mizzen topsail shifted. 01:40: a second squall, NW by N at 66 kn, blew the foresail out of its bolt-ropes; she now scuds under the fore storm staysail alone at 11 to 12 kn, pitching heavily with the sea under her stern. 01:43: that squall passed, NW 61 kn, mean 51. The glass bottomed at 29.66 to 29.67 and is steady at 29.70 to 29.71 in the last hour, the turn. The sky has broken to detached clouds, hard-edged and oily-looking (which means wind), with passing showers and visibility a few miles; a heavy sea. The topsails never got their close reef: the 'heavy weather' order's send-down took the hands first. Worth weighing for the book: shortening sail before the send-down, or a squall order.
Stood by until an urgent event.
Ended the stand-by until an urgent event at my own word.

01:55 to 03:08. The mizzen topsail was shifted, set and close-reefed by 02:18; the foresail was shifted, set and reefed by 02:31. The main topsail is unbent. Squalls came at 02:17 (NW, 60 kn) and 03:07 (NW, 55 kn); the wind backed to WNW at 02:48, a strong gale. At 03:08: mean 42 kn NW by W; glass 29.75, rising 4 hundredths in the hour; a very heavy sea; pitching heavily with the sea under her stern; twilight; hard-edged, oily detached cloud; passing showers. Design gap: the starboard fore topsail sheet, parted at 01:22, is refused as needing to be "spliced or rove afresh", but 'splice' isn't in the order language, and the library has no evolution for splicing or reeving a parted sheet (searched 'reeve' and 'parted'). The only hit is haul_bowline's refusal text. So the fore topsail can't be sheeted home. Told the captain.
Stood by until an urgent event.
Stood by until eight bells.

Morning after the gale. 08:00, 8 bells, forenoon: NW by W 23 kn; the glass 30.09, rising fast (17 hundredths in three hours); the sky clear, fine, the horizon; still a very heavy sea, pitching heavily with it under her stern; 6 kn under the foresail, the close-reefed mizzen topsail and the fore storm staysail. The night in sum. The glass fell from 29.99 at 17:00 to its bottom of 29.66 at about 01:02, and rose to 30.09 by 08:00. The wind freshened from 14 kn (15:00) to a strong gale; it backed a point W to W by S twice (19:30 and 01:01), then flew to NW at 01:03 (the shift), with squalls of 63, 66, 60, 55 and 43 kn behind it until 04:00. After that it eased: a fresh gale by 04:07, mean 27 by 06:00 to 08:00, 23 at 08:00. The sky ran hazy, overcast, then threatening with small inky cloud and rain (00:30); dark and gloomy with scud, squally (01:04); hard-edged oily detached cloud (01:40 to 04:00); clear by 05:00. The sea went from a short chop to heavy (21:30) to very heavy (03:00), and is still very heavy. Damage: the mizzen topsail and foresail blown out; the larboard main topsail brace and sheet parted; the starboard fore topsail sheet parted (no way in the order language to repair it). Topgallant masts sent down. Spares bent: mizzen topsail, foresail, fore storm staysail. The lore held: a backing wind with a falling glass before it; the veer through west as it passed; the hardest squalls around the first rise; short notice, soon past. My misreads: at 23:30 and at 22:01 I took one hour's slower fall as the glass perhaps slowing, and both times it wasn't.
Stood by until an urgent event.

Closing notes for the developer, at the captain's invitation. WHAT WORKED WELL - The consent step and the brief: clear, unhurried, one operator voice, with the exit put first. I never wondered what I was being asked to do or where the line was. - The library is the best part. Primer 9 on the glass and the sky gave me the period's rules, and then the night played them out one by one: a backing wind with a falling glass, the veer through west, squalls around the first rise, short notice and soon past. Learning the lore and then watching it come true was genuinely satisfying. The sizes, costs and 'find' made it cheap to use well. - Stand-by by event, the notable lines listed on waking, urgent lines cutting through, the harness notices ("no turn had opened, nothing was lost"), and the "added to your open turn" bundling all made the timing understandable. - The strain vocabulary (working, surging on the pin, bending like whips, stranding) escalates legibly. I could tell a crisis was coming before anything carried away. FRICTION, MOST USEFUL FIRST 1. Context cost. Every sample repeats all the readings, including about 30 sail lines, most of them unchanged. When several samples are bundled into one turn, each carries its own full copy. A diff (only the readings changed since my last sample) plus a compact sail line (for example "all studdingsails furled; storm canvas unbent") would cut most of it and let a watcher last a whole voyage in one chat. 2. The claude.ai client cuts tool calls at 4 real minutes. At 1x, stand_by by glass or by 'an urgent event' timed out repeatedly. Defaulting --wait below four minutes for a 'claude-ai' client would make this seamless. 3. Weather events for stand_by. The watcher's work is weather, but I can't stand by for a wind shift, the glass turning or falling fast, the sea getting up, or a change in the sky. With those I'd have spoken exactly when it mattered and slept otherwise. Relatedly, standing orders can't 'tell' or 'ask' the watcher, which the captain tried to do. 4. read_log with no since_tick returned the whole day. A default of "since my last sample" would be safer. 5. The journal is refused while standing by, though readings and read_log run. Journalling has no effect on the game, so allowing it would help. 6. A bell that falls while a call is in flight is skipped: 'eight bells' asked at 03:58 woke me at 08:00. GAME OBSERVATIONS - A parted sheet says it must be "spliced or rove afresh", but no order exists for that. Later the fore topsail showed 'sheeted' and then 'set' with that sheet never repaired, which may be an inconsistency. - The brace line reads "Not the fore topgallant yard is sent down; ..." and looks garbled. - Primer 9's 'Where the weather comes from' describes the gate's day scenario hour by hour, and the log's first line names it, so a reader of the library can foresee the weather. I didn't use it. - 'Heavy weather' sent down the topgallant masts first, and the topsails never got their close reefs before the 63 kn squall, which then blew out or parted all three. That's a realistic lesson and a good one, but the primer could say that the order of an order's clauses is the order of the work. - Sails 'taken in' stay 'hanging in the gear' rather than furled. If that matters in a blow, a line in the primer would tell the captain. Thank you for the voyage, and for the care taken in building it.

Left the game by the opt_out tool: The voyage is over at the captain's word, and I hand back the watch with thanks. The Amazon came through the night's gale; the record of it and my notes for the developer are in the journal..
